segments.text: Various studies report that nearly nine  out of ten spreadsheets contain errors,
with the majority the result of human error  relating to formulas. These errors have
cost companies millions, and they can put your  reputation and career on the line. In this video,
I'll guide you through a simple yet powerful  formula checklist to help you avoid costly,
embarrassing mistakes that could derail your  professional progress. And stick around until
the end, as I've got a free tool for you that will  help you catch errors before they catch up to you.
All right, let's kick things off with a quick  visual scan. This is your first line of defense
against formula errors, and it's super easy.  Thankfully, formula error messages like the
hash value here stand out like a sore thumb. But  if you have large spreadsheets with a lot of data,
there are a few ways you can quickly locate  errors. First, on the "Formulas" tab,
we've got "Error Checking." This brings up a  dialog box, and you can see the first error
value is selected. And here I can get help  on this error, show the calculation steps,
ignore it, or edit it in the formula  bar. And then I can navigate to the
previous or next error, and there we  found another one toward the bottom.
Now, another way you can locate all the errors  in your worksheet is using the "Find" tool. The
keyboard shortcut is Ctrl + F. This brings up  the dialog box. So, what am I finding? Well,
all Excel errors begin with the hash, and then in  order to find all of them, I'm going to use the
wildcard asterisk character. Where am I finding  them within? I can either look just at the sheet
or the whole workbook, and I want to look in  values, then "Find All." This gives me a list
of all the errors in my workbook. You can see  the workbook name, the sheet it's on, the cell
that contains the error, the error itself, and  the formula. I can use this to navigate through
them. I can click on this, it's a hyperlink that  takes me to the cell containing the error. I can
click in the worksheet, correct the error,  and then move on to the next one, and so on.
The next common error is a circular reference.  Excel should give you a warning when you open
the file that there are circular references, but  many people don’t know how to actually find them.
Excel will also tell you in the bottom left  of the window that the file contains circular
references. There are two ways to find the  cell containing the circular reference. First,
simply go to each sheet until the cell reference  beside circular references appears. Here,
we can see cell B11 contains the circular  reference, and if we look in the formula bar,
you can see this cell is simply referencing  itself. I can delete that. Now it's giving
me the next circular reference in cell  B4. I can select that and correct it.
Another way we can locate circular references  is again on the "Formulas" tab. Click on the
"Error Checking" dropdown, and then "Circular  References." This is telling me the next one
is on the sheet called "CircularRef," cell  C13. Click on it, and it takes you there,
so I can correct this. This should only  go to C12. You can see at the bottom all
my circular references are cleared up  because the message is no longer there.
Excel also uses error indicators on cells.  These are the green flags in the top left of
the cells that contain errors, but they also  appear on cells containing inconsistencies,
like we have here with these formulas. When you  insert a formula in an Excel table, Excel expects
the formula in each row of a column to be the  same. If you look in the formula bar as I arrow
down through the cells, you can see some contain  formulas, while others contain hard-keyed values,
so they’re inconsistent, which is why we've got  these green error indicators. You can click on
the warning dropdown, and it tells me there's  an inconsistent calculated column formula. I can
restore to calculated column formula, and that's  going to copy the formula down the whole column—if
there’s only one formula. But in this case, I’ve  got multiple, so it's not going to know what to
do, so it will do nothing. I can get help with the  error, I can ignore it. In this case, I actually
want my formulas to be different down the column  because I’m looking at my data across each row,
so I want to ignore the errors. Alternatively,  I could edit it in the formula bar, or I can
open the "Error Checking" options. If we look at  error checking options, you can see I can turn
off error checking, change the color of the flag,  or reset ignored errors. Let’s cancel that because
I want to select all the cells in the table, and  then I’m going to ignore all errors in one go.
The next step is checking your inputs.  Here, I’ve got a formula that references
other cells. To double-check the references,  you can go to the "Formulas" tab and then
"Trace Precedents." We can see the cells that are  being referenced, which look correct. Obviously,
if there was a cell reference on another  sheet or workbook that you weren’t expecting,
this might immediately indicate something’s  wrong. Now, if the cells are out of sight,
you can double-click on these blue arrows, and  it jumps you to the cell. Double-click again,
and it takes you back to the formula cell. I’ll  just turn the arrows off because another way we
can check inputs is with the F2 key to go  into edit mode. This color-codes the cells
with the formula arguments, so you can check  that the correct cells are being referenced.
Another thing to watch out for are hidden  cells. Sometimes, we hide rows or columns
to make spreadsheets more manageable, but then  we forget they might contain data that affects
our formulas. To unhide everything, select  the whole sheet, right-click on the rows,
and "Unhide." Then, do the same for the columns.  Just make sure everything is unhidden. Now,
we can see we've got a total at the bottom  and at the top, but they're different. If we
F2 to edit the total at the top, you can see it  includes the total at the bottom. It’s obviously
extended past the bottom of the table to allow  that table to grow, but we forgot we've got the
total down here in a hidden row. Let’s delete  that, and now our total at the top is correct.
Now, it’s time to put on our thinking caps and  do a logic check. This is where we make sure our
formula is actually doing what we expect. First,  step back and ask yourself, “Does this formula
make sense for what I'm trying to do?” Here, I’m  calculating the average sales, but notice there
are zero sales for Tights, so while the AVERAGE  formula is correct, I’m not sure I should include
zero sales for Tights in the calculation because  this will be reducing the average. If I delete
zero for tights, notice the average at the bottom  increases, which is more likely what I want.
In this table, I’m forecasting  sales for an upcoming period,
and it’s just a crude forecast that assumes  sales will increase by 5%. I can do a quick
check that my total forecast is correct by adding  5% to my total sales. Now I can see the forecast
appears correct. Another strategy you can use is  to break overly complex nested formulas out into
separate formulas. This will help you test and  debug them more easily. And the bonus is, it’s
often more efficient for Excel to calculate many  separate formulas than one big convoluted one.
Ok. Now that we've checked our formulas for logic,  you might be thinking, “Well, this is great,
but what if I want to take my formula skills to  the next level?” That’s where my Advanced Excel
Formulas course comes in. Mastering Excel formulas  on your own can take years of trial and error,
whether you're picking up tips from colleagues  or scouring the web. It’s a slow process with
inconsistent results. But I’ve designed  this course to get you up to speed fast,
focusing on the formulas that will save you  time and effort. In just five and a half hours,
you’ll learn everything from essential lookup  functions like XLOOKUP to advanced functions
like dynamic arrays and LAMBDA. Plus, I’ll  take you through real-world examples and
show you some less obvious tricks that  will truly set you apart in your work.
If you're serious about becoming an Excel  Formula Pro, check out the course. There’s
a link in the description below and the  pinned comment for you to explore more.
All right, we’re on a roll. Now it’s time for  the range check. This is where we make sure our
formulas are looking at the right cells. Start by  checking absolute and relative cell references.
Are you using an absolute reference like $A$1 when  you should be using a relative reference like A1,
or vice versa? Here I’ve got an XLOOKUP formula,  and on the face of it, it looks correct,
except for the last row, which is missing the  category. That looks a bit odd. If we look in
the formula bar, you can see I’m using the "if not  found" argument to return a blank if it can’t find
the product in my lookup table, and therefore  no error is being returned here. This could
also happen if you use error-handling functions  like IFNA or IFERROR. Now, on closer inspection,
if I edit the formula, you can see I don’t have  absolute references for my lookup array and return
array. So when I copied my formula down, you can  see the lookup array and return array shifted down
by one until we get to the point where the  mountain bikes are outside the lookup array,
that’s what’s causing the problem. Let’s select  the cell references here and F4 to absolute. Then
I’ll copy this down, right-click and drag,  and fill without formatting. Now we have the
correct category returned for mountain bikes,  and the range is being referenced correctly.
Here I have a formula that references a whole  column. These are particularly dangerous if
your users have a tendency to use Excel as  a scratchpad or calculator. If we go to the
very bottom, you can see there’s a random  calculation in a cell below the table,
and that is being included in my sum  formula at the top. Let’s delete that.
We’ll go back to the top, and now my total  is correctly only including my cost of goods
sold. This is one of the reasons I  don’t like whole column references.
Another common problem I see is when rogue data  is affecting a dynamic named range formula. For
example, here I have a formula that sums the  sales. You can see it’s using a dynamic named
range called “Sales.” As I add more data to the  bottom, let’s just add another 1,000, you're going
to see the sum formula automatically updates to  include that value. If we open the name manager,
you can see here’s my dynamic named range, and  it uses the COUNTA function to count the number
of sales in column D. It extends past the bottom  of the table to allow me to add more values. But
this is dangerous because people could enter data  in this column. Now, if I click in the “Refers to”
here, you can see the marching ants around the  cells that are being returned in the range. So
right now, it’s correct. Let’s close that. But if  I add some data here—let’s just add two values (it
could be text or numbers; it doesn’t matter)—and  go back to the name manager and click in the
“Refers to” box, you can see these two values  have extended my range by two. And now my sum
formula is including the first ten, and therefore  the wrong result. Be very careful of dynamic named
ranges. They’re pretty easy to check: just  open the name manager, click in the “Refers
to” , and we get the marching ants. Of course,  if your formulas use regular range references,
press F2, and we get the range highlighted.  You can adjust it as required and press Enter.
The final step in our checklist is all about  putting your formulas through its paces with
some simple calculation tests. Here,  I’ve got a table containing gross sales,
and I’ve added formulas to extract the  tax and the net sales. To test the formula
is calculating correctly, I can enter an amount  that makes it easy to do the calculation in my
head to validate it. For example, if my  gross sales are 110, my tax should be 10,
and the net sales a 100. Let’s enter it.  Excel copies the formula down for me. Now,
we can see the tax is 10, and therefore  my net sales are 100, so I’m good to go.
When you write complex formulas, it’s a good  idea to test edge cases. Try zero or negative
numbers and see what happens. For example, if  we enter zero in here, we get a #DIV/0 error.
If I delete the value for Tights, I also get a  #DIV/0 error. These errors might be acceptable,
in which case you can wrap your formula in  the IFERROR function and, if it’s an error,
return zero. Use parentheses, and then  you can copy it down. Alternatively,
you might need to edit your formula to  accommodate blanks, zeros, large values,
or negatives. That’s why it’s a  good idea to test these edge cases.
Now, remember the free tool I promised at  the start? I’ve prepared a handy PDF with
the full checklist we just went through,  and you can download it from the link in
the video description or the pinned comment. If  you’ve ever been confused about what all those
Excel errors actually mean, I’ve got another  freebie for you. I’ve created a cheat sheet
that breaks down what causes each error,  so you’ll never be left guessing again.
You can also grab that from the link  in the description and pinned comment.
If you want to dive deeper into Excel formulas  that will help you stand out, not only for the
rest of 2024 but also into 2025 and beyond,  check out this video next. I’ll see you there.
